guideTitle: 6 Best Wide Power Lift Recliners in 2026
metaTitle: Best Wide Power Lift Recliners for 2026
metaDescription: Six wide power lift recliners for broader frames, compared on stated seat width, capacity, motors and footprint, with sizing and delivery advice.
introParagraphs: A wide power lift recliner exists for people who find standard chairs tight at the hips or the arms. Wide can mean a seat of 24 to 26 inches, an overall width of 40 inches or more, or simply an extended backrest, and listings mix those meanings freely. That makes numbers essential, because a chair that is wide in marketing language may not be wide where your body needs the room.

We evaluated six chairs from their product pages, comparing stated seat widths, overall dimensions, capacity where given, motor layout and the comfort extras on offer. Everything is based on product specs and buyer feedback, not hands-on use. A lift chair is a seating product, and how well any size or lift suits you varies by person, so an occupational therapist can advise on transfers and fit.

Only two listings here publish firm numbers for both size and capacity, so expect to verify the rest on the product page. Treat any missing figure as a question to answer before ordering, not as a reason to guess.

products.name: CANMOV 46 Inch Wide Oversize Power Lift Recliner

specList.label: Dimensions
specList.value: 39 L x 46 W x 42 H in

products.description:
This CANMOV is the widest chair in the group by stated numbers: 39 inches long, 46 inches wide and 42 inches high, with a listed maximum weight capacity of 450 pounds. The motor moves it through four positions, and the maker says it handles the transitions even under heavy weight. Eight massage points plus two heating points sit behind a five-level timer.

A 46 inch overall width is a lot of furniture, and it will dominate a small living room. The excerpt does not state the seat width separately, so the usable seat is something to confirm. Four positions rather than infinite adjustment is simpler to operate but offers fewer fine postures.

Plan the delivery path, because a 46 inch chair needs wide doorways and a clear hallway. Next to the CUZSIT, which lists a 24.5 inch seat, this CANMOV lists capacity and outside size instead. Choose it when a published weight figure is the deciding factor.

products.name: CUZSIT Oversized Power Lift Recliner
products.description:
The CUZSIT lists a 24.5 inch seat width, which the maker says is two to three inches wider than most recliners, in a body described as space-saving. A constant-speed lifting system aims for steady, gentle movement, and a two-button control keeps the operation as simple as a wide chair can get. Double-layer springs and high-density foam form the cushion.

The two-button approach is its biggest strength for someone who dislikes busy remotes. It is also its limit, as the listing mentions few comfort extras and the seat is narrower than the 26 inch chairs. Weight capacity does not appear in the excerpt.

Setup is the standard outlet plus clearance routine for a lift chair. Against the Zuacs at 26 inches, the CUZSIT is a bit narrower but easier to operate and more compact overall. It suits someone who needs a wider-than-standard seat without a showroom-sized chair.
products.bestFor: A buyer who wants a wider seat with the simplest possible two-button controls.

products.name: Zuacs Dual Motor 26 Inch Extra Wide Lift Chair
products.description:
The Zuacs offers a 26 inch seat, the broadest stated seat in this guide, on a dual-motor frame that lets the backrest and footrest move separately. An automatic telescopic footrest extends for longer legs, and a manual headrest has three settings at 10, 25 and 35 degrees. Flip-up arms open to reveal storage for remotes and glasses.

The manual headrest is the tradeoff: it adjusts by hand, so you cannot change it from the seat with a button. The flip arm storage is a genuine daily convenience for keeping small items near. Weight capacity is not stated in the excerpt, which is an important number for a chair aimed at larger users.

In a room it takes serious space and an outlet within reach. Compared with the FUNECORP, which also uses dual motors, the Zuacs lists a seat width and storage, while the FUNECORP lists lumbar heat and massage modes. Choose the Zuacs if width and storage matter most.

products.name: FUNECORP Big Man Power Lay Flat Lift Recliner
products.description:
FUNECORP builds an extra-wide chair on dual Okin motors, so the backrest and footrest adjust separately and the chair can lay flat. Eight massage units run in five named modes, with a lumbar heating element alongside. The maker positions it for larger users and for seniors who need help standing.

Naming the motor brand is a small point in its favor, since buyers can look up the supplier's reputation. The cons are the same as many in this group: no seat width and no capacity figure in the excerpt. It is also heavy, so the delivery path must be planned.

Once in place it needs an outlet and room for lay-flat recline. Compared with the CANMOV 46 inch, the FUNECORP gives mode names but no weight limit, while the CANMOV gives the limit but fewer motor details. Pick it when massage and lay-flat matter and you can verify size elsewhere.

products.name: CANMOV Large Power Lift Recliner With Extended Backrest
products.description:
This CANMOV is aimed at big and tall users, with an extended backrest for taller sitters and a widened seat for broader frames. One remote controls the lift and the recline, and eight points of massage with heat come in five modes. The maker says it moves smoothly at the push of a button.

The extended backrest is the feature that sets it apart, since many wide chairs only add width without adding height. The excerpt does not give seat width or weight capacity, and the remote carries more controls than a two-button unit. Confirm the numbers on the product page before treating wide as a safe description.

It asks for the usual room, outlet and doorway planning. Compared with the CUZSIT, this CANMOV offers backrest height and five massage modes, while the CUZSIT offers a stated 24.5 inch seat and fewer controls. Choose by whether you are tall, broad or both.

products.name: MCombo Dual Motor Power Lift Recliner R7897 Medium-Wide
products.description:
The R7897 is the most modest chair here, labelled medium-wide rather than oversized, with dual motors, infinite positions and a zero gravity setting. The maker says its lift system is TUV certified and describes it as helping with standing.

That medium-wide label is honest but narrower than the 24 to 26 inch chairs. It will suit someone who finds standard seats snug but not someone who needs a very broad frame. As with most excerpts, seat width and capacity are not given.

It installs like any lift chair, with outlet access and clearance. Next to the Zuacs, it offers the certified lift wording but less width. It is a sensible middle step for a household that wants lift assistance and a bit of extra room without a showroom-sized recliner.

buyingCriteria.explanation: A wide chair can have thick arms that eat most of the width. Focus on the seat: the CUZSIT lists 24.5 inches and the Zuacs lists 26 inches, against typical seats of 20 to 22 inches. Add a few inches to your hip measurement while seated for comfort. The CANMOV 46 inch lists 46 inches overall but no seat figure, so overall width alone can mislead.

Capacity should include clothing and anything in your lap. The CANMOV 46 inch is the only listing here that states a maximum, 450 pounds. The others leave it out of the excerpt, so check the product page. Do not infer capacity from words like heavy-duty or big man.

Wide chairs can exceed 44 inches boxed and 46 inches when assembled, as on the CANMOV 46 inch. Measure every door, turn and stair on the route, and compare against the shipping dimensions on the page. A chair that cannot get in is a costly mistake. White-glove delivery, where offered, is worth reading about.

The CUZSIT keeps things to two buttons, while the FUNECORP and Zuacs use dual motors for separate back and footrest movement. More motors add posture options and more controls. For a wide chair that you will use daily, simplicity can outweigh variety. Choose the layout you can operate without looking.

Broader users are often taller too, and a short footrest or backrest undermines the width. The Zuacs has an automatic extended footrest and the CANMOV with an extended backrest addresses height. Check your lower leg and torso lengths against the product page. A wide seat with short support still feels wrong.

Makers describe lift in different ways, from the MCombo R7897's certified system to the CUZSIT's constant-speed lift. None of this confirms the chair suits your transfers. An occupational therapist can advise, and a trial in a showroom can help if one is available.

howWeEvaluated.title: Width figures
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked for stated seat and overall widths. The Zuacs lists 26 inches, the CUZSIT lists 24.5 inches and the CANMOV 46 inch lists 46 inches overall. Chairs without a measured number were treated as unverified.

howWeEvaluated.title: Capacity and build
howWeEvaluated.description: We checked weight capacity and frame details. Only the CANMOV 46 inch states a capacity at 450 pounds, while the CUZSIT lists double-layer springs and the FUNECORP names its Okin motors. Capacity gaps were flagged for verification.

howWeEvaluated.title: Controls and motors
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared the control approach. The CUZSIT uses two buttons, the Zuacs and FUNECORP use dual motors, and the CANMOV 46 inch uses four positions. We credited simple controls for ease and dual motors for flexibility.

howWeEvaluated.title: Comfort extras
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at heat, massage and storage. The FUNECORP lists five named modes, the CANMOV 46 inch adds a five-level timer, and the Zuacs adds flip arm storage. These tipped close decisions.

howWeEvaluated.title: Lineup positioning
howWeEvaluated.description: The CANMOV 46 inch leads on capacity and total size, the Zuacs on seat width, the CUZSIT on simplicity, and the MCombo R7897 on moderate size with certified wording. Our picks follow those strengths.

faq.q: How wide should a seat be for a larger user?
faq.a: Measure your hips seated and add a few inches. Typical seats run 20 to 22 inches, and wide chairs like the CUZSIT at 24.5 inches and the Zuacs at 26 inches go beyond that. Check arm thickness too. The posted seat width is more useful than the overall width.

faq.q: Is the CANMOV 46 inch too big for a normal room?
faq.a: At 46 inches wide and 39 inches long it needs a generous room. Measure the footprint and the reclined length. The product page is the final word on clearances. A smaller option like the CUZSIT may suit tighter spaces.

faq.q: Why do some listings omit weight capacity?
faq.a: Many makers put it in a specification sheet rather than the bullet points. Always check the product page for the posted figure. Include clothing and lap items in your estimate. Do not assume a wide chair carries a high limit.

faq.q: Do wide lift chairs need special delivery?
faq.a: They are heavy and bulky, so measure doorways and stairwells first. Some chairs need around 44 inches of clearance when unboxed. Look at the shipping dimensions on the page. Some sellers offer in-home delivery, which may help.

Many people find it easier. The CUZSIT uses two buttons for lift and recline, which keeps things simple. If you want separate backrest and footrest control, look at dual-motor chairs like the Zuacs. Choose the layout you can operate without looking. Large, clearly separated buttons also help anyone with stiff or less sensitive fingers, so check how the remote is shaped and whether it has a place to rest on the arm.

faq.q: Are massage and heat useful in a wide chair?
faq.a: They are comfort extras, not substitutes for fit. The FUNECORP lists five named modes and the CANMOV 46 inch adds a five-level timer. A pharmacist or doctor can advise if you have skin or circulation concerns about heat. Prioritize size and capacity first.

faq.q: Will a wide lift chair suit my transfers?
faq.a: That depends on your body and your movement. Makers describe lift in different ways, and none of it guarantees suitability. An occupational therapist can advise before you buy. A showroom trial can help if available.
